bull_bear.body:
- Execution/ramp risk acknowledged as the residual risk (demand, capacity, manpower largely de-risked via multi-year contracts and qualifications).
- Elevated working capital / inventory build; cash-flow conversion dependent on plant utilization ramping FY27+.
- Front-ended depreciation & finance costs rising from heavy FY26 capex.

- Middle East geopolitics: viewed as a macro risk, "business as usual"; Saudi plant timeline shifted due to regional situation.
- Organizational restructuring — selectively replacing functional leaders outgrown by scale (key-person/transition risk).

bull_bear.body:
- MHI hot-section nozzle vanes were previously made in-house by MHI — now single-sourced to Azad; positions Azad directly against Howmet/PCC in a ~3-player global niche.

- Nuclear is an existing, already-qualified revenue stream (EDF/Arabelle), not just a theme — rare qualified nuclear-turbine-airfoil capability in India.
- ~96% inventory <1yr old reframes the "elevated inventory" optics as forward-stocking, not obsolescence.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Customer and segment concentration — Energy and Oil & Gas contributed 81.5% of FY 2025-26 revenue, concentrated among three OEMs; revenue is weighted towards a small number of large global OEMs and rebalancing through Aerospace & Defence and Oil & Gas is a multi-year undertaking.
- Qualification dependency — Qualification status depends on sustained quality and delivery performance; withdrawal by a major OEM would remove revenue that could not be substituted in a comparable timeframe given multi-year requalification cycles.
- Programme conversion timing — A meaningful part of the order book depends on timely conversion of qualified programmes into production volume, which is subject to timeline variability given the technically demanding, often first-of-kind components and systems.
- Working capital and capex intensity — Working capital and capital expenditure requirements are expected to stay structurally elevated as capacity expands ahead of full utilisation; sustained free cash flow is expected to develop only gradually, and return ratios lag until new lines contribute from FY 2026-27.
- Export and end-market cyclicality, trade and geopolitics — Revenue is heavily export-weighted, exposing the Company to cycles in commercial aerospace production, energy-sector capex and defence procurement; evolving trade policy may affect input costs, logistics and customer procurement timelines.
- Input dependency and raw material pricing — Customer-mandated raw materials come from a limited pool of approved mills, restricting supplier substitution and negotiation; raw material cost is passed through but the Company absorbs price movement within a ±5% band.
- Talent scarcity and ramp-up execution — Precision machining and process engineering talent is scarce; retention and capability transfer are prerequisites to ramping new dedicated facilities on schedule.
- Technological progression — Rising component complexity requires sustained investment in process capability and equipment to hold qualification standing on next-generation programmes.

outlook.body: AZAD is executing a two-phase, customer-dedicated capacity build-out tied to firm contracted customer commitments rather than anticipated demand. Since listing it has inaugurated four dedicated lean manufacturing facilities: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (March 2025), GE Vernova and Siemens Energy (commissioned during FY 2025-26), and Baker Hughes (April 2026, at the Tuniki Bollaram campus, its first in Oil & Gas). Phase 1 is progressing as per schedule, creating incremental capacity of ~95,000 sq. m; the build-out was roughly 70% to 80% complete at year end, with the rest to be closed by FY 2026-27, and further phased capacity is under construction. On completion of both phases the manufacturing footprint reaches approximately 182,000 square metres, roughly nine times the area at the start of the expansion, spread across all three verticals and dedicated to specific OEM programmes. Expansion and working capital were funded through internal accruals, debt and QIP equity; management expects capital efficiency to improve as the new facilities reach normalised utilisation, with substantive contribution from the new lines expected from FY 2026-27.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- The constraint on output across all three end markets has moved to the supply side: OEM order books lengthened while qualified capacity in high-temperature alloy forging, precision machining and specialist coating expanded far more slowly.
- OEMs are contracting further forward, consolidating volumes with already-qualified suppliers and increasingly underwriting dedicated capacity instead of ordering against periodic purchase orders.
- Gas turbine demand driven by electricity demand growth from electrification, industrial load and AI data-centre build-out; delivery slots at the largest turbine makers are committed several years forward.
- Installed-base replacement of rotating and stationary components on maintenance cycles provides demand independent of the investment cycle.
- Nuclear generation back on the policy agenda (life extension, restarts, new build, SMRs); in India, planned nuclear additions and opening to private participation extend demand domestically.
- Aerospace: multi-year airframe and engine backlogs constrained by supply chain; fleets flown longer lift shop visits and spare component demand.
- Defence: budgets shifting to multi-year procurement and to unmanned/loitering systems that need expendable propulsion units; India pressing indigenisation of propulsion and aero-engine development.
- Oil & Gas: a wave of LNG liquefaction capacity under construction gives turbomachinery vendors multi-year backlogs; oilfield equipment demand moving toward more severe-duty, tighter-tolerance applications.
- Hot-section nozzle vane category opens a large addressable market and carries better return metrics than historical categories.
- Mix is diversifying: airfoils fell from close to 90% of Energy output four years ago to ~75% in FY 2025-26 as the Company qualified adjacent component categories.
- Order book of approximately ₹65,000 million as at March 31, 2026, approximately 11 times FY 2025-26 revenue; a management estimate of contracted and committed work, not audited.
- By vertical: Energy roughly 57% (~₹37,000 million), Aerospace & Defence about 29% (~₹18,500 million), Oil & Gas about 14% (~₹9,500 million).
- OEM contracts across sectors average five to six years in tenure.
- Mitsubishi Heavy Industries: Phase 2 of the rotating and stationary airfoil contract signed, taking combined Phase 1 and Phase 2 value to ₹13,870 million over a five-year execution period; plus an eight-year single-source Long Term Contract and Price Agreement (March 2026) for hot-section nozzle-vane segments.
- GE Steam Power GmbH (GE Vernova): Long-Term Supply Agreement for rotating and stationary airfoils for nuclear, industrial and thermal power, valued at approximately USD 53.5 million.
- Baker Hughes (Nuovo Pignone S.r.l.): Strategic Supply Agreement amended in May 2025, extending it through 2030 on a significant increase in annual demand.
- Pratt & Whitney Canada: Master Terms Agreement and Purchase Agreement concluded in December 2025; Safran Aircraft Engines: Memorandum of Understanding; Rolls-Royce: seven-year contract awarded January 2024, under qualification.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- The constraint on output across all three end markets has moved to the supply side: OEM order books lengthened while qualified capacity in high-temperature alloy forging, precision machining and specialist coating expanded far more slowly.
- OEMs are contracting further forward, consolidating volumes with already-qualified suppliers and increasingly underwriting dedicated capacity instead of ordering against periodic purchase orders.
- Gas turbine demand driven by electricity demand growth from electrification, industrial load and AI data-centre build-out; delivery slots at the largest turbine makers are committed several years forward.
- Installed-base replacement of rotating and stationary components on maintenance cycles provides demand independent of the investment cycle.
- Nuclear generation back on the policy agenda (life extension, restarts, new build, SMRs); in India, planned nuclear additions and opening to private participation extend demand domestically.
- Aerospace: multi-year airframe and engine backlogs constrained by supply chain; fleets flown longer lift shop visits and spare component demand.
- Defence: budgets shifting to multi-year procurement and to unmanned/loitering systems that need expendable propulsion units; India pressing indigenisation of propulsion and aero-engine development.
- Oil & Gas: a wave of LNG liquefaction capacity under construction gives turbomachinery vendors multi-year backlogs; oilfield equipment demand moving toward more severe-duty, tighter-tolerance applications.
- Hot-section nozzle vane category opens a large addressable market and carries better return metrics than historical categories.
- Mix is diversifying: airfoils fell from close to 90% of Energy output four years ago to ~75% in FY 2025-26 as the Company qualified adjacent component categories.
- Order book of approximately ₹65,000 million as at March 31, 2026, approximately 11 times FY 2025-26 revenue; a management estimate of contracted and committed work, not audited.
- By vertical: Energy roughly 57% (~₹37,000 million), Aerospace & Defence about 29% (~₹18,500 million), Oil & Gas about 14% (~₹9,500 million).
- OEM contracts across sectors average five to six years in tenure.
- Mitsubishi Heavy Industries: Phase 2 of the rotating and stationary airfoil contract signed, taking combined Phase 1 and Phase 2 value to ₹13,870 million over a five-year execution period; plus an eight-year single-source Long Term Contract and Price Agreement (March 2026) for hot-section nozzle-vane segments.
- GE Steam Power GmbH (GE Vernova): Long-Term Supply Agreement for rotating and stationary airfoils for nuclear, industrial and thermal power, valued at approximately USD 53.5 million.
- Baker Hughes (Nuovo Pignone S.r.l.): Strategic Supply Agreement amended in May 2025, extending it through 2030 on a significant increase in annual demand.
- Pratt & Whitney Canada: Master Terms Agreement and Purchase Agreement concluded in December 2025; Safran Aircraft Engines: Memorandum of Understanding; Rolls-Royce: seven-year contract awarded January 2024, under qualification.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: AZAD is executing a two-phase, customer-dedicated capacity build-out tied to firm contracted customer commitments rather than anticipated demand. Since listing it has inaugurated four dedicated lean manufacturing facilities: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (March 2025), GE Vernova and Siemens Energy (commissioned during FY 2025-26), and Baker Hughes (April 2026, at the Tuniki Bollaram campus, its first in Oil & Gas). Phase 1 is progressing as per schedule, creating incremental capacity of ~95,000 sq. m; the build-out was roughly 70% to 80% complete at year end, with the rest to be closed by FY 2026-27, and further phased capacity is under construction. On completion of both phases the manufacturing footprint reaches approximately 182,000 square metres, roughly nine times the area at the start of the expansion, spread across all three verticals and dedicated to specific OEM programmes. Expansion and working capital were funded through internal accruals, debt and QIP equity; management expects capital efficiency to improve as the new facilities reach normalised utilisation, with substantive contribution from the new lines expected from FY 2026-27.
